extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism and intellectual history; students and general readers interested in assessing public intellectuals and philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative literary-criticism criteria for judging a public intellectual (here: Jeremy Bentham) focusing on originality, method, style, practical applicability, and moral psychology. Useful for reviewers assessing the merits and defects of philosophical/political works for a general or professional readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal intellectual influence vs. local reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: His reputation 'lies at the circumference' — known little in England, better in Europe, best abroad; his reasonings, if true, 'are true everywhere alike'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the subject's ideas have universal applicability and influence beyond local/political contexts (intellectual reach across nations and times), rather than being merely locally or temporally significant. Consider examples such as offering constitutions for other countries or corresponding with foreign sovereigns as evidence of wide influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and discovery versus arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'has not struck out any great leading principle...'; 'His forte is arrangement; and the form of truth, though not its essence, varies with time and circumstance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine intellectual invention (new principles, immortal truths) and skill in organizing, collating, or systematizing existing materials. Value originality higher for lasting contribution; treat excellent arrangement as useful but potentially transient (books of reference liable to be superseded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of a single governing principle (e.g., Utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'has assumed the principle of UTILITY as the foundation of just laws...'; but 'he has carried this single view of his subject too far' and reduced human life to calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reliance on one overarching principle oversimplifies complex moral/social phenomena. Check for over-extension of an abstract principle without allowances for human variety, imagination, and emotion; prefer theories that make room for collateral aids, habits, and other moral faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for human nature and agent capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: In ascertaining rules of moral conduct 'we must have regard... to the capacity of the agent'; pleasures are not 'equally a good' because they differ on reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge theories and prescriptions by how well they consider actual human psychology, capacities, passions, and the role of sympathy and imagination. Theories should distinguish immediate pleasures from those that bear reflective approval and should adapt to agents' practical limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between reason/logic and sentiment/imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'has been led... to consider man as a logical animal' and at times 'reduced the theory and practice of human life to a caput mortuum of reason'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author's method over-intellectualizes human affairs, neglecting sympathy, sentiment, and imaginative aspects that shape moral behavior. Good argumentation integrates rational calculation with emotional and habitual elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, accessibility, and intelligibility of style
rubrics_metrics.description: His style 'is unpopular, not to say unintelligible... a barbarous philosophical jargon' — 'his works... ought to be translated into English.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prose for clarity, plainness, and reach to intended readers. Technical jargon, elliptical cypher-like sentences, excessive parentheses, and law-Latin reduce accessibility; prefer writing that communicates to its audience without needless obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity and prioritization in argument (valuation not inventory)
rubrics_metrics.description: His reasoning is 'rather like an inventory, than a valuation of different arguments' — 'Every possible suggestion finds a place, so that the mind is distracted as much as enlightened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor authors who weigh and prioritize arguments rather than cataloguing every possible point equally. Good criticism or theory distinguishes between the importance and the number of items; avoid a dispersed method that obscures central claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applicability to the subjects of reform (empirical grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjusting penal codes he 'lays too little stress on the co-operation of the natural prejudices of mankind' and lacks knowledge of criminals' principles of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether proposed reforms are grounded in empirical observation and an understanding of the people affected (e.g., criminals). Practical success requires consulting relevant experience (reformed offenders, turnkeys, prisons) rather than pure armchair reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability of behavioural change beyond controlled conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Panopticon: will a convert 'work when he is from under Mr. Bentham's eye... keep sober' once surveillance is removed? 'The charm of criminal life... consists in liberty... excitement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether prescribed interventions create lasting change or only temporary compliance under supervision. Consider motivational factors (liberty, excitement, social identity) that may cause relapse outside controlled environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longevity and lasting contribution versus temporary usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: His writings are 'chiefly valuable as books of reference' which are 'constantly liable to be superseded', whereas a 'truth discovered is immortal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between work that is a useful contemporary compendium and work that offers enduring theoretical discoveries. Prioritize substantive, novel contributions that are likely to outlast fashions and scaffolding of current knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of method and tone to the intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'a technicality of manner, which renders his writings of more value to the professional inquirer than to the general reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the author's level of technicality, style, and methodological choices fit the audience. Professional detail can be an asset for specialists but alienate general readers; effectiveness depends on intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of over-elaboration and inflated self-importance
rubrics_metrics.description: He writes 'as if he was allowed but a single sentence to express his whole view... as if, should he omit a single circumstance... it would be lost to the world for ever.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of authors who overstate the necessity of each detail and cram excessive minutiae into argumentation. Effective communication often requires concision and recognition that language need not encode every possible contingency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical engagement rather than armchair speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'What should Mr. Bentham, sitting at ease... know of the principles of action of rogues, outlaws, and vagabonds? No more than Montaigne of the motions of his cat!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value first-hand knowledge, empirical examples, and engagement with lived experience when assessing social or penal theories. Theorists detached from their subject matter risk irrelevant or implausible prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral valuation beyond simple pleasure aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bentham's view that 'Every pleasure... is equally a good' is contested: 'All pleasure is not, therefore (morally speaking) equally a good; for all pleasure does not equally bear reflecting on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral theories on whether they account for qualitative differences among pleasures and the role of reflection and conscience. Simple quantification of pleasures can misrepresent moral worth; consider reflective approval and long-term effects.
